source.title: Random matrix analysis of deep neural network weight matrices
source.authors: M. Thamm; Max Staats; B. Rosenow

record.tranche_reason: Reports test accuracies for fully connected and convolutional networks trained on CIFAR-10, but does not test the original claim's random-label memorization comparison or the specified local-connectivity interventions.
record.gate_note: The paper measures trained weight-matrix statistics and reports classification accuracies. Its RMT statistics do not measure the magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance in V7. The cited random-label and double-descent findings are prior work, not this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study's own CIFAR-10 results bear on V3: miniAlexNet outperforms four fully connected networks trained from scratch with momentum SGD. This is an architecture comparison with different regularization, rather than an intervention isolating local connectivity.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors interpret image-classification weights as a random bulk plus learned low-rank contributions, and find the best tested generalization between rich and lazy learning. Their conclusion also rejects a generic single-power-law description of spectral tails. They acknowledge that agreement with RMT does not guarantee absence of learned information; lazy networks may require analysis of weight changes rather than final weights.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes trained weight matrices with random-matrix statistics and reports classification accuracies; it does not reproduce the original claim's random-label experiment or its specified interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported CIFAR-10 test accuracy varies across architecture and seed. In the MLP512 learning-regime comparison, test accuracy varies with laziness parameter α.

fits_no_version.finding: Trained weight matrices retain random-matrix spectral statistics, while singular vectors associated with large singular values show deviations from randomness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random-matrix analysis can distinguish random bulk structure from candidate learned low-rank structure in image-classification networks.

fits_no_version.finding: MLP512 test accuracy is 52.7%, 55.2%, and 50.4% in the rich, typical, and lazy regimes, respectively.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Among these tested learning regimes, intermediate learning yields the highest held-out accuracy.

record.problems: The CIFAR-10 MLP and miniAlexNet accuracy comparison is not a controlled comparison isolating convolution or local connectivity; model architectures and regularization differ. The paper reports no uncertainty for the listed test accuracies. Its weight-statistics results do not directly measure training–test error gaps.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the table's training accuracies or the pretrained ImageNet models: they do not add a matched convolution-versus-fully-connected comparison for V3. The layer-wise spectral-statistics results across additional networks and regimes are not extracted exhaustively; the selected R6–R7 rows capture the central reported weight-statistics findings.

untested.parts: No random-label fitting or random-versus-natural-label held-out comparison.
No width sweep beyond an established interpolation threshold with training to convergence.
The contribution of local connectivity, learned sparse local connections, convolutional initialization of fully connected networks, and datasets other than CIFAR-10 are untested.
No adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparison or tuning comparison.
No magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance, correlation with generalization gaps, or ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
No removal of memorized examples and retraining against a random-removal control.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V3. Its incidental architecture comparison supplies supporting evidence, with no uncertainty reported for these accuracies. The regularization difference limits causal attribution, but does not itself demonstrate a condition where V3 fails.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of held-out performance on random versus natural labels.
No width sweep past the zero-training-error threshold; the reported MLP sizes are not a test of the specified width claim.
Does not test learned sparse local connections, convolutional initialization of fully connected networks, or the cited MNIST, CIFAR-100 and SVHN settings.
No batch-size comparison or fixed-epoch large-batch test.
Measures random-matrix statistics of weights, not magnitude-scaled weight-perturbation tolerance or its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
No removal of memorized training examples.

rows.subject: MLP512 (second hidden layer)
rows.operation_detail: Compared unfolded singular-value spacings with the GOE Wigner surmise.
rows.measure: Kolmogorov–Smirnov test p-value for spacing distribution
rows.value: p-value 0.40; null hypothesis cannot be rejected at significance level α = 0.40
rows.note: This is a weight-statistics result, not a measure of the gap between training and test error.
rows.check: Spectral spacing agreement measures none of the claim versions. Table I gives p = 0.401; Section II reports non-rejection at alpha = 0.40, rather than explicitly reporting an exact p-value of 0.40.

rows.subject: MLP512 (second hidden layer)
rows.operation_detail: Compared singular-vector entries with the Porter–Thomas Gaussian distribution using KS tests; averaged p-values over neighboring singular values.
rows.baseline: Gaussian distribution with zero mean and standard deviation 1/√m
rows.value: Most eigenvectors, especially those belonging to small singular values, are consistent with randomness; p-values decrease for large singular values.
rows.note: The paper interprets the high-singular-value deviations as indicating stored information; this does not test V7's sharpness measure.
rows.check: Singular-vector randomness does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or any other listed version.
